children: Shares of Mosaic
and Nutrien

briefly declined Monday after President Donald Trump said the United States is working on a major agreement to buy potash from Belarus at prices substantially below those currently paid for Canadian supplies.
The market reaction reflected the potential competitive threat from bringing more Belarusian potash into North American and global fertilizer markets. Mosaic
and Nutrien
are major potash producers, while Belarus is one of the world's biggest sources of the crop nutrient.

“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. He said the pricing would be “substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada,” describing the potential agreement as good news for U.S. farmers and ranchers.
Trump didn't provide details on potential purchase volumes, timing, transportation arrangements or pricing.
Investor takeaway
For investors, the immediate reaction in Mosaic
and Nutrien
underscores concern that additional low-cost Belarusian supply could pressure potash prices and producer margins. Mosaic
has substantial exposure to potash alongside its phosphate business, while Nutrien
is one of the world's largest potash producers. CF Industries
, by contrast, is primarily a nitrogen fertilizer producer, making its direct exposure considerably smaller.

The near-term impact may be limited. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said Monday that the country has little potash available for Western buyers because essentially all of its 2026 production is already committed under existing contracts.
That makes the announcement potentially more significant for expectations about 2027 and beyond than for fertilizer supplies during the remainder of this year.
Belarus could add competition

Potash provides potassium, one of the three major nutrients used in commercial fertilizer along with nitrogen and phosphorus. Canada dominates U.S. imports and is the world's largest potash producer, while Belarus is another major global supplier.

Belarusian potash exports have faced restrictions and logistical obstacles stemming from Western sanctions. The country has redirected much of its trade toward Russia, China and other Asian markets. Lukashenko said Monday that 85% of Belarusian exports and imports are now moving eastward.

Washington and Minsk have been discussing potash as part of broader negotiations that have included sanctions relief and the release of prisoners. Recent talks have also involved frozen Belarusian assets and other economic issues.
A significant return of Belarusian production to Western markets could increase competition even if much of the material doesn't ultimately enter the United States.
Potash is globally traded, meaning additional supply in one region can influence benchmark prices and redirect cargoes elsewhere.
